title: Selected Work
subtitle: Dense interfaces, prototypes engineering ships from, and the decisions I defended through the build

bio.short: I design B2B software and run the product side too. The spec, the board, the customer call. Five years of that was data-dense analytics for banks and insurers at Datameer. More recently a vertical ERP at ChurchDesk, where I was one of two designers with no design org above me. I prototype in real code against real APIs, and engineering ships from it.
bio.long:
Start with ChurchDesk. I held product management for the platform and all of its design at the same time. I wrote the specs, ran the ticket board the two engineers worked from, and was the parish's main contact throughout. A client asked for a funeral-booking feature. The €20k was already committed and the deal closed before I joined. I was brought in to lead it. Internally the plan was a standalone add-on module; I built the booking capability into the platform instead and held that line to delivery. It cut coordination time by 70% and ran at 90% acceptance at the launch customer, where funerals had to be bookable across 20+ cemeteries. It then shipped to every customer as a general booking capability, for room rentals and weddings as much as funerals.

The interface craft comes from Datameer. Five years of big-data pivot tables, column charts, aggregated JSON views, result cards and filter logic. The users were analysts inside top US, Canadian and UK banks and insurers, on a platform operating under HIPAA compliance among other frameworks. The hardest surface was the query-builder preview. The result you are looking at is a sample, the interface has to be honest about that, and it still has to stay readable.

Now at Bibel TV I prototype in real code against real APIs, web first and then Android, and engineering ships from that code. Around 70% of what the model writes lands. Iteration moved from days to hours. Engineering there is an external agency, so that handoff crosses a company boundary and still holds. I write the specs, run the board, and check the built feature in production and beta rather than calling it done at handoff. I don't review their pull requests.

context.company: Secfix — compliance automation for European SMBs, certifying against ISO 27001, GDPR, TISAX and SOC 2 by pulling evidence out of a company's tech stack. The posting states €17M in total (€12M Series A). Small: the engineering team recently doubled and this is the second designer.
context.role: Senior Product Designer, in the Engineering department, reporting to the co-founder and CTO. An IC seat with full product ownership. No PMs, so the designer writes the specs, runs the ticketing workflow and decides what ships. Staff/Principal in scope by the posting's own words.
context.emphasis: Lead with three things in this order. One: prototypes in real code that engineering ships from, crossing a company boundary. Two: designer and product manager at once — the specs, the ticket board, the customer calls, and a scope decision defended through the build with a number attached. Three: dense interface craft from Datameer — tables, filters, data density. Write 'I' throughout, never 'we'. Name no colleague on this page.
context.avoid: Facts to hold exactly. Interface craft is tables, filters, query-builder previews and data density; permissions, roles, access control and settings pages are outside what he has designed, so claim none of them, and Ninox's user-built data models are a different problem from an access matrix. Compliance experience is GDPR plus Protestant and Catholic church data-protection law — not ISO 27001, SOC 2 or TISAX. Engineering copies and adapts parts of his prototype code, edits them, then ships; he does not review pull requests. The tool is Claude Code. Lead with the work rather than with headcount. State no compensation figure.
